records.title: Change in Tandem
records.text:
Change in Tandem
How input values and output values of a function vary together: domain and range, increasing and decreasing, concavity, and zeros.
A function is a rule that relates two changing quantities. Describing how the output values change as the input values change, whether they increase or decrease and whether the rate of change is increasing or decreasing, is the starting point for every function in this course.
Unit 1 is built on two ideas: covariation, meaning how output values change in tandem with input values, and rates of change. This topic is about the first idea, and it introduces the precise language the AP Exam expects whenever you describe a function.

1.1.A · A function maps each input value to exactly one output value.
Each input value has exactly one output value. Images are output values, and preimages are sets of input values.
A function is a mathematical relation that maps a set of input values to a set of output values so that each input value is mapped to exactly one output value. The set of input values is the domain, and the set of output values is the range. The variable that represents input values is the independent variable, and the variable that represents output values is the dependent variable.

The preimage of an output value is the set of all input values that give it: the preimage of 3 is {0, 1}.
Two functions f and g are equal only when they have the same domain and f(a) = g(a) for every input value a in that domain. A function can be given graphically, numerically (a table), analytically (a formula), or verbally (a description). The representation changes, but the function does not.

records.text:
1.1.A · Increasing and decreasing compare output values as input values increase.
State the interval, then say how the output values change as the input values increase.
A function f is increasing over an interval of its domain if, as the input values increase, the output values always increase. That is, for all a and b in the interval, if a < b, then f(a) < f(b). A function is decreasing over an interval if, as the input values increase, the output values always decrease: for all a and b in the interval, if a < b, then f(a) > f(b).

records.heading: 1.1.B · A zero is an input value where the output value is zero.
records.text:
1.1.B · A zero is an input value where the output value is zero.
A zero is an input value. The output value at a zero is 0.
The graph of a function intersects the x-axis when the output value is zero, and the corresponding input values are the zeros of the function. If p(x) = (x − 2)(x + 5), then p(2) = 0 and p(−5) = 0, so the zeros of p are x = 2 and x = −5, and the graph crosses the x-axis at the points (2, 0) and (−5, 0).
Analytically: set the output equal to 0 and solve.
Numerically: look for table rows whose output value is 0.
Graphically: look for the input values where the graph meets the x-axis.
Verbally: ask when the measured quantity equals 0, such as when a height reaches the ground.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.text:
Rates of Change
Average rates of change over intervals, rates of change at a point, and what the sign of a rate of change says about how two quantities vary together.
Rates of change quantify how two quantities vary together. An average rate of change describes an interval, and average rates of change over smaller and smaller intervals approximate the rate of change at a point.
Topic 1.1 described whether output values increase or decrease. This topic measures how fast they do. Average rate of change, with units and an interpretation, appears in nearly every modeling free-response question on the AP Exam.
records.excerpt: Average rates of change over intervals, rates of change at a point, and what the sign of a rate of change says about how two quantities vary together.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.2.A · The average rate of change is a ratio of changes over an interval.
records.text:
1.2.A · The average rate of change is a ratio of changes over an interval.
Average rate of change = (change in output values)/(change in input values), stated for an interval and with units.
The average rate of change of a function f over the interval a ≤ x ≤ b is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a), the ratio of the change in the output values to the change in the input values. It is the constant rate of change that would give the same change in output values as f gives over that interval. Its units are output units per input unit.

records.title: Rates of Change
records.heading: 1.2.B · The sign of a rate of change describes how two quantities vary together.
records.text:
1.2.B · The sign of a rate of change describes how two quantities vary together.
Interpret a rate of change with its sign, its size, its units, and its interval or point.
A positive rate of change means that as one quantity increases or decreases, the other quantity does the same.
A negative rate of change means that as one quantity increases, the other decreases.
The size of a rate of change tells how much the output values change per unit change in the input values.
A rate of change can be positive at some points and negative at others, and an average rate of change over a long interval can hide those changes. An average rate of change of −0.5 degrees Celsius per minute for cooling coffee means that, on average, the temperature decreased by 0.5 degrees Celsius per minute over that interval. It does not mean the temperature fell at that rate every minute.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.text:
Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
Average rates of change for sequences, linear functions, and quadratic functions, secant lines, and how the change in average rates of change reveals concavity.
The pattern of average rates of change over consecutive equal-length input-value intervals identifies a function type. Constant average rates of change mean linear. Average rates of change that change at a constant rate mean quadratic.
Topic 1.2 computed and interpreted average rates of change. This topic studies how those average rates of change themselves change, which is the reasoning the AP Exam expects when you justify a choice of model from a table.

records.title: Rates of Change in Linear and Quadratic Functions
records.heading: 1.3.A · The average rate of change over [a, b] is the slope of a secant line.
records.text:
1.3.A · The average rate of change over [a, b] is the slope of a secant line.
Average rate of change over [a, b] and the slope of the secant line are the same number.
The average rate of change of a function f over the closed interval [a, b] is the slope of the secant line from the point (a, f(a)) to the point (b, f(b)). For f(x) = x², the secant line from (1, 1) to (3, 9) has slope (9 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 4, which is also the average rate of change of f over [1, 3].
Different intervals give secant lines with different slopes unless the function is linear. That is a picture of why only a linear function has a constant average rate of change.

records.heading: 1.3.B · The change in the average rates of change reveals concavity.
records.text:
1.3.B · The change in the average rates of change reveals concavity.
Increasing average rates of change mean concave up, and decreasing ones mean concave down.
For a linear function, the average rates of change over consecutive equal-length intervals are given by a constant function, so they change at a rate of zero. For a quadratic function, they are given by a linear function, so they change at a constant rate.
When the average rate of change over equal-length input-value intervals is increasing for all small-length intervals, the graph of the function is concave up. When it is decreasing for all small-length intervals, the graph is concave down.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
Degree, leading term, and leading coefficient, relative and absolute extrema, extrema between real zeros, and points of inflection.
Where the rate of change of a polynomial function changes sign, the function has a relative maximum or minimum. Where the rate of change changes from increasing to decreasing, or the reverse, the graph has a point of inflection.
Topics 1.1 to 1.3 described output values and rates of change in general. Polynomial functions are the first family where those ideas combine into several turning points and changes in concavity on one graph.

records.heading: 1.4.A · A polynomial function has a degree, a leading term, and a leading coefficient.
records.text:
1.4.A · A polynomial function has a degree, a leading term, and a leading coefficient.
Write the terms from highest to lowest power: the first term is the leading term, and its power is the degree.
A nonconstant polynomial function of x is any function representation equivalent to p(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀, where n is a positive integer, each aᵢ is a real number, and aₙ is nonzero. The polynomial has degree n, the leading term is aₙxⁿ, and the leading coefficient is aₙ.

records.text:
1.4.A · Relative extrema occur where a polynomial switches between increasing and decreasing.
A relative extremum is greatest or least nearby. An absolute extremum is greatest or least over the whole domain.
Where a polynomial function switches between increasing and decreasing, or at an included endpoint of a polynomial with a restricted domain, the function has a local, or relative, maximum or minimum output value. If a relative maximum is greater than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, maximum. If a relative minimum is less than all other output values, it is a global, or absolute, minimum.

1.4.A · Between two distinct real zeros there is a relative extremum.
Two distinct real zeros guarantee at least one relative extremum between them, not exactly one.
Between every two distinct real zeros of a nonconstant polynomial function, there must be at least one input value corresponding to a relative maximum or relative minimum. The output values leave 0 and return to 0, so the function must change direction in between.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
Zeros and linear factors, multiplicity, complex zeros and conjugates, degree from successive differences, and even and odd functions.
The zeros of a polynomial function, counted with multiplicity, determine its linear factors, where its graph crosses or is tangent to the x-axis, and the endpoints of the intervals where it is positive or negative.
Topic 1.4 showed that relative extrema sit between real zeros. This topic studies the zeros themselves, including non-real zeros that never appear on the graph but still count toward the degree.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: 1.5.A · A real number a is a zero of p if and only if (x − a) is a linear factor of p.
records.text:
1.5.A · A real number a is a zero of p if and only if (x − a) is a linear factor of p.
Real zeros give linear factors, x-intercepts, and the endpoints of the intervals where p(x) > 0 or p(x) < 0.
If a is a complex number and p(a) = 0, then a is a zero of the polynomial function p, or a root of the equation p(x) = 0. If a is a real number, then (x − a) is a linear factor of p if and only if a is a zero of p, and the graph of y = p(x) has an x-intercept at the point (a, 0). For example, p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3), so the real zeros of p are 1, −2, and 3.
Real zeros of a polynomial can be endpoints for intervals satisfying polynomial inequalities. To solve p(x) > 0, find the real zeros, then determine the sign of p(x) on each interval between them.

records.heading: 1.5.A · A repeated linear factor gives a zero with multiplicity.
records.text:
1.5.A · A repeated linear factor gives a zero with multiplicity.
Even multiplicity: same sign on both sides and tangent to the x-axis. Odd multiplicity: the sign changes and the graph crosses.
If a linear factor (x − a) is repeated n times, the corresponding zero has multiplicity n. A polynomial function of degree n has exactly n complex zeros when multiplicities are counted. For p(x) = (x + 1)²(x − 2)³, the zero −1 has multiplicity 2, the zero 2 has multiplicity 3, and the degree is 5.
If a real zero a has even multiplicity, then the signs of the output values are the same for input values near x = a, and the graph is tangent to the x-axis at x = a. If a has odd multiplicity, the output values change sign and the graph crosses the x-axis.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
records.heading: 1.5.A · Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
records.text:
1.5.A · Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.
Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs, and every zero counts toward the degree.
A complex number has the form a + bi, where a and b are real and i² = −1. If a + bi is a non-real zero of a polynomial function p, then its conjugate a − bi is also a zero of p. For example, x² − 2x + 5 has zeros 1 + 2i and 1 − 2i.
Non-real zeros are not x-intercepts, but they count toward the degree. The function p(x) = (x² + 4)(x − 1) has degree 3 and three complex zeros, 2i, −2i, and 1, but its graph has only one x-intercept, at (1, 0). Because non-real zeros come in pairs, a polynomial of odd degree has at least one real zero.

records.title: Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
records.text:
Polynomial Functions and End Behavior
Limit notation for end behavior and why the degree and the sign of the leading term determine the end behavior of a polynomial function.
As input values increase or decrease without bound, the leading term of a polynomial dominates all lower-degree terms. So the degree and the sign of the leading term determine the end behavior.
Zeros and extrema describe the middle of a polynomial's graph. End behavior describes the output values as the input values increase or decrease without bound, and the AP Exam expects it in limit notation.

records.heading: 1.6.A · End behavior is written with limit notation.
records.text:
1.6.A · End behavior is written with limit notation.
The input direction goes under lim, and the output behavior goes after the equals sign.
As the input values of a nonconstant polynomial function p increase without bound, the output values either increase without bound or decrease without bound. The corresponding notation is lim x→∞ p(x) = ∞ or lim x→∞ p(x) = −∞. As the input values decrease without bound, the output values also either increase or decrease without bound: lim x→−∞ p(x) = ∞ or lim x→−∞ p(x) = −∞.

records.text:
Rational Functions and Zeros
The real zeros of a rational function, and how the real zeros of its numerator and denominator determine where it is positive or negative.
The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of its numerator that are in its domain. The real zeros of the numerator and of the denominator together mark the endpoints and asymptotes of the intervals where the function is positive or negative.
A quotient is 0 only when its numerator is 0 and the quotient is defined. That single fact gives the zeros of a rational function and is the starting point for solving rational inequalities.

records.heading: 1.8.A · The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of the numerator in its domain.
records.text:
1.8.A · The real zeros of a rational function are the real zeros of the numerator in its domain.
Find the real zeros of the numerator, then discard any that are not in the domain.
The real zeros of a rational function correspond to the real zeros of the numerator for such values in its domain. For r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 3)/(x − 1), the real zeros are x = 2 and x = −3. The value x = 1 makes the denominator 0, so 1 is not in the domain of r.
For r(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x − 1), the numerator is 0 at x = 1 and x = −1, but x = 1 is not in the domain of r. The only real zero of r is x = −1. Topic 1.10 describes the graph at x = 1.

Where the graph of a rational function has a vertical asymptote, and how one-sided limits describe the output values near it.
Near a real zero of the denominator that is not cancelled by the numerator, the denominator's values are arbitrarily close to 0, so the output values of the rational function increase or decrease without bound.

records.heading: 1.9.A · A vertical asymptote occurs at a real zero of the denominator that is not a zero of the numerator.
records.text:
1.9.A · A vertical asymptote occurs at a real zero of the denominator that is not a zero of the numerator.
Compare the multiplicity of each real zero of the denominator with its multiplicity in the numerator.
If a is a real zero of the polynomial in the denominator of a rational function and is not also a real zero of the polynomial in the numerator, then the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = a. A vertical asymptote also occurs at x = a if the multiplicity of a as a real zero of the denominator is greater than its multiplicity as a real zero of the numerator.
For r(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 3), the denominator is 0 at x = 3 and the numerator is 4 there, so the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 3. For (x − 1)/(x − 1)², the value 1 has multiplicity 2 in the denominator and 1 in the numerator, so there is a vertical asymptote at x = 1 as well. The domain of each function leaves out the asymptote's x-value.

Rational Functions and Holes
When the graph of a rational function has a hole instead of a vertical asymptote, and how a limit locates the hole.
A rational function can be undefined at x = c without a vertical asymptote. If the multiplicity of c as a real zero of the numerator is at least its multiplicity in the denominator, the output values approach a single value L and the graph has a hole at (c, L).
Topic 1.9 compared multiplicities to find vertical asymptotes. This topic covers the other outcome of that comparison, and it uses a two-sided limit to give the coordinates of the hole.

records.text:
Equivalent Representations of Polynomial and Rational Expressions
Factored and standard forms, polynomial long division, and the binomial theorem, and which form answers which question.
Equivalent analytic representations of the same function reveal different information. Factored form shows real zeros, holes, asymptotes, domain, and range. Standard form shows end behavior. Long division gives slant asymptotes, and the binomial theorem expands powers of binomials.
Earlier topics factored to find zeros, holes, and vertical asymptotes, and compared leading terms to find end behavior. This topic names those forms and adds two tools the CED requires: polynomial long division and the binomial theorem.

records.text:
1.11.B · Polynomial long division gives f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x).
The quotient gives the slant asymptote, and the remainder term approaches 0 at the ends.
Polynomial long division is an algebraic process similar to numerical long division, involving a quotient and a remainder. If the polynomial f is divided by the polynomial g, then f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where q is the quotient, r is the remainder, and the degree of r is less than the degree of g. Dividing by g(x) gives f(x)/g(x) = q(x) + r(x)/g(x).
To divide x² + 3x + 5 by x − 1: x · (x − 1) = x² − x, leaving 4x + 5; then 4 · (x − 1) = 4x − 4, leaving a remainder of 9. So x² + 3x + 5 = (x − 1)(x + 4) + 9, and (x² + 3x + 5)/(x − 1) = x + 4 + 9/(x − 1).
The result of polynomial long division is helpful in finding equations of slant asymptotes. As x increases or decreases without bound, 9/(x − 1) gets arbitrarily close to 0, so the slant asymptote is y = x + 4.

Use row n for the coefficients, and raise the whole of a and b, signs included, to their powers.
The binomial theorem uses the entries in a single row of Pascal's triangle to expand expressions of the form (a + b)ⁿ, including polynomial functions of the form p(x) = (x + c)ⁿ, where c is a constant. records.text:
Transformations of Functions
Additive and multiplicative transformations: translations, dilations, and reflections, combined transformations, and their effect on domain, range, and asymptotes.
Adding a constant to the input or output of a function translates its graph, and multiplying the input or output by a constant dilates it, possibly with a reflection. Changes to the input act horizontally, and changes to the output act vertically.
Each function type in AP Precalculus comes with a parent function. Transformations turn a parent function into a model that fits a context, which is why they appear in modeling questions throughout the course.

records.title: Transformations of Functions
records.heading: 1.12.A · Additive transformations translate the graph.
records.text:
1.12.A · Additive transformations translate the graph.
f(x + h) translates horizontally by −h units. f(x) + k translates vertically by k units.
The function g(x) = f(x) + k is an additive transformation of f that results in a vertical translation of the graph of f by k units. The function g(x) = f(x + h) is an additive transformation of f that results in a horizontal translation of the graph of f by −h units.

records.heading: 1.12.A · Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined.
records.text:
1.12.A · Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined.
Work from the inside out: find the input to f, then apply the dilation and translation of the output.
Additive and multiplicative transformations can be combined, resulting in combinations of horizontal and vertical translations and dilations. The set of points before the transformations is the preimage, and the set of points after the transformations is the image.
Let f(x) = x² − 1, with zeros at x = −1 and x = 1, and let g(x) = 2f(x − 3). The graph of g is the graph of f translated horizontally by 3 units and dilated vertically by a factor of 2. The zeros move to x = 2 and x = 4, and the vertex (0, −1) moves to (3, −2).
When transformations are given in words, build the rule one step at a time. A horizontal dilation by a factor of 2, then a vertical dilation by a factor of 3, then a vertical translation by 5 units gives g(x) = 3f(x/2) + 5. To evaluate g(4), find f(4/2) = f(2) first.
g(x) = 3f(x/2) + 5, so g(4) = 3f(2) + 5. Show the input value given to f before applying the outside operations.

records.heading: 1.12.A · A transformation can change the domain, the range, and the asymptotes.
records.text:
1.12.A · A transformation can change the domain, the range, and the asymptotes.
Transform the asymptotes, the domain, and the range along with the points.
The domain and range of a function that is a transformation of a parent function may be different from those of the parent function. Horizontal transformations move vertical asymptotes and change the domain. Vertical transformations move horizontal asymptotes and change the range.
The parent function f(x) = 1/x has the vertical asymptote x = 0 and the horizontal asymptote y = 0. For g(x) = 1/(x − 2) + 3, the asymptotes are x = 2 and y = 3, the domain is all real numbers x ≠ 2, and the range is all real numbers y ≠ 3. The parent function x² has range y ≥ 0, while h(x) = −2x² + 3 has range y ≤ 3.

records.text:
Function Model Selection and Assumption Articulation
Choosing a linear, quadratic, polynomial, or piecewise-defined model from a data set or context, and stating the assumptions and domain and range restrictions of a model.
A function model is chosen by matching how the quantities in a data set or context change to how a function type changes. Every model also carries assumptions about what stays consistent, and restrictions on its domain and range.
You now know how linear, quadratic, and other polynomial functions change. This topic asks which type to choose and how to justify the choice, a part that appears in free-response Question 1 and Question 2 of the AP Exam.

Use a piecewise-defined model when the rate or pattern changes at a known input value.
A piecewise-defined function consists of a set of functions defined over nonoverlapping domain intervals. It is useful for modeling a data set or contextual scenario that demonstrates different characteristics over different intervals.

State the assumption, the domain, and the range in the language of the context.
A model may assume something is consistent, such as a constant growth rate or a fixed price.
A model may assume how the quantities change together, such as a constant rate of change for a linear model.
A model may require domain restrictions based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.
A model may require range restrictions, such as rounding to whole numbers, based on mathematical clues, contextual clues, or extreme values in the data set.

Translations place the vertex or asymptotes; one more point fixes the dilation.

records.text:
1.14.B · Inversely proportional quantities are modeled by rational functions.
Inverse proportionality gives a rational model k/x or k/x². Asymptotes describe long-run values.
Data sets and contextual scenarios involving quantities that are inversely proportional can often be modeled by rational functions. For example, the magnitudes of the gravitational force and the electromagnetic force between objects are inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, and so is the intensity of light from a point source.
If the intensity of light is 50 lux at 2 meters from a source and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance d, then I(d) = k/d² with 50 = k/4, so k = 200 and I(d) = 200/d². At d = 5 meters the model predicts I(5) = 8 lux.
